Davidson County by the numbers

Which Metro offices deal with a Davidson County tax bill?

Two Metro Nashville offices split the job. The Assessor of Property appraises and classifies every parcel, while the Office of the Metropolitan Trustee sends the statements and takes the payments. The Trustee has no authority over the amount of an assessment.

Each September the Trustee receives the certified roll from the Assessor. The Trustee's office is in the Howard Office Building at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220, open weekdays from 8 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon. The Assessor's office takes value questions at 615-862-6080.

Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville are the only cities in Davidson County that bill separate city taxes. Their numbers are 615-297-6041, 615-859-0596 and 615-851-2200. Taxes for every other city address are collected by the Metropolitan Trustee.

What is the Davidson County payment calendar?

Statements go into the mail during the first week of October. Payment opens the first Monday of that month, and the full amount has to be in by the final day of February if you want to skip interest.

Because today is November 15, 2026, the 2026 bill is already out and the cutoff arrives in late February 2027. You may pay in installments along the way.

Miss the cutoff and interest of 1.5% (18% a year) is added to the base tax on the first of every month, beginning March 1. The Trustee's collections division works delinquent accounts from March through the following February, and after that the Clerk and Master's office collects them.

How do payments reach the Metropolitan Trustee?

Options include the Trustee's website, the mail, and the counter at the Howard Office Building. Payments sent through your own bank's bill pay count on the day the Trustee receives them.

  • Make checks payable to Metropolitan Trustee, PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
  • Cards cost 2.35% of the payment, with a $2.00 floor, and an E-Check costs $1.00. Metro keeps none of it.
  • A postmark sets the payment date for mail, but a private meter stamp does not. With no postmark, the day the envelope arrives counts.
  • A website payment is credited on the day you make it.

The Trustee's pages call out that new owners should check their closing statement or ask the title company who owes the tax, because unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property.

What changed in the 2025 reappraisal?

The Assessor's final countywide median value increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025. Notices were mailed April 18, 2025, four years after the previous reappraisal in 2021, and the Assessor said owners were being given more time than usual to appeal.

State law requires a Certified Tax Rate after each reappraisal so that local governments do not collect a windfall on existing property. The 2025 rates came to $2.782 per $100 in the General Services District and $2.814 per $100 in the Urban Services District, down from $2.922 and $3.254 in 2024.

2025$2.782$2.814
2024$2.922$3.254
2021$2.953$3.288
2020$3.788$4.221

Source: Davidson County Assessor, Tax Rates and Calculator. The Urban Services District pays for garbage pickup, street lights and sidewalks that owners in the General Services District arrange on their own.

How do you work out a Davidson County bill?

Multiply the appraised value by the 25% residential ratio and apply the rate for your district. The Assessor's own example uses a $400,000 house in the Urban Services District: $400,000 times 25% is $100,000 of assessed value, and at $2.814 per $100 the bill is $2,814.00.

Your notice shows a Tax Jurisdiction box that says whether you are in the GSD, the USD or one of the satellite cities. Those are Ridgetop, Goodlettsville, Belle Meade, Berry Hill, Forest Hills and Oak Hill, and their owners pay the GSD rate plus the city's own rate. Downtown properties may also sit inside the Central Business Improvement District or the Gulch Business Improvement District, which add their own assessments.

What is the path to contest a Davidson County value?

The Assessor handles an informal review first. A formal appeal then goes before an independent hearing officer or the Metropolitan Board of Equalization, scheduled through the Assessor's call center at 615-862-6059.

For the 2025 cycle, informal reviews had to be requested by May 9 and formal appeals scheduled by 4:00 p.m. on June 27. The Assessor warned that owners who miss the formal deadline may lose their right to appeal for that tax year. Those dates are past, so a challenge today applies to a future year.

During an appeal the Trustee says to pay at least the undisputed share before delinquency, along with any past-due prior-year tax. To find the undisputed portion, divide the value you claim by the Assessor's value and multiply by the tax due. A final certificate of assessment brings either a refund or a balance owed with interest at the Federal Reserve composite prime rate minus two points.

What tax relief can a Davidson County owner claim?

The state reimburses local taxes for low-income elderly or disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans, and the Trustee runs a tax freeze for owners 65 and older. Eligibility turns on age or disability, ownership and residency, and income.

  • Elderly and disabled relief: applicants must turn 65 by December 31 of the tax year or be disabled by that date, and must document ownership with a bill, deed or probated will.
  • Disabled veterans: a 100% disability rating is required, there is no income limit, and relief covers the first $175,000 of market value.
  • Tax freeze: owners 65 and older who live in the home can freeze the bill at the amount for the year they qualify. Applications are due by April 5 each year, and the Trustee's number is 615-862-6330.

Income caps on the Trustee's page are stated for the 2020 calendar year, so ask the Trustee for the current limits before you apply.

What does Nashville-Davidson look like for a seller?

Davidson County is governed as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson County. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 745,904 residents, up 4.2% from April 2020, spread over 503.70 square miles of land at roughly 1,421 per square mile.

Census QuickFacts shows the following figures for 2020 to 2024:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $417,400.
  • Share of housing lived in by owners: 52.8%, which leaves renters near half of households.
  • Median gross rent: $1,582.
  • Median household income: $77,853.
  • Households: 324,907, in 389,379 housing units as of July 2025.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 5,632.

Source: Census QuickFacts. The Register of Deeds, Karen Johnson, is at 300 Deaderick Street in Nashville and records deeds for sales anywhere in the county.

What happens to a delinquent Davidson County parcel?

Delinquent parcels can end up in a tax sale auction run through Chancery Court. Auctions are held one Wednesday a month starting in June, and sales are final, but the owner has a one-year right to redeem the property. The buyer earns 10% annual interest on the purchase price during the redemption period.

The Trustee's page says the county does not help purchasers with any foreclosure or eviction. Anyone running behind should phone the Trustee's collections division before March 1 for a payoff figure, and a seller should hand that number to the title company.

More questions about Davidson County, TN Property Tax Guide

When is Davidson County property tax due?

Statements go out the first week of October, taxes are payable from the first Monday of October, and the full amount must be paid by the last day of February to avoid interest. Interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1.

What is the Davidson County property tax rate?

For 2025 the General Services District rate is $2.782 per $100 of assessed value and the Urban Services District rate is $2.814, according to the Assessor. Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville bill separate city taxes on top of the GSD rate.

How much did Davidson County values rise in the 2025 reappraisal?

The Assessor's final countywide median increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025. Council district medians ranged from 38% to 54%. The Certified Tax Rate was then set to keep revenue on existing property level.

Does Davidson County accept partial property tax payments?

Yes. The Trustee accepts partial payments during the collection period, but the full balance must be paid by the last day of February to avoid interest. Cards carry a 2.35% fee with a $2.00 minimum, and E-Check costs $1.00.

Who pays the property tax when a Davidson County house is sold?

The closing statement answers that. The Trustee tells new owners to check it or ask the title company, because payment depends on when the property is transferred and unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property.

Knox County by the numbers

Which Knox County offices deal with property tax?

Two offices share the job, both in the Knoxville City-County Building at 400 Main Street. The Property Assessor, reachable at 865-215-2360, sets values and fields appeal questions. The Trustee, in Suite 427 at 865-215-2305, takes the payments. Each keeps weekday counter hours that start at eight and end at half past four. The Assessor's separate line for business personal property is 865-215-2362.

The Trustee's payment page lists six locations, plus these ways to pay:

  • Online through the county's property tax lookup, with a 2.5% processing fee on cards and $1.00 on e-checks
  • By phone at 865-215-2305, option 3
  • By mail to P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901

The Trustee describes its office as one that collects and accounts for over $1 billion a year in state, federal and local funds, so the same counter that takes a homeowner's check also handles county government's money. The Trustee's office also accepts address changes online, and the Assessor takes mailing address changes at 865-215-2360.

What is Knox County's tax rate this year?

The county finance page says taxes for fiscal 2026 are levied at $1.5540 per $100 of assessed value, set by the County Commission as part of the budget. Residential property is assessed at 25% of value, commercial at 40% and business personal property at 30%, and the Assessor's FAQ shows the formula: assessed value times the percentage times the combined city and county rate.

Take a house appraised at $300,000. A quarter of that is $75,000 of assessment, and at $1.5540 per $100 the county tax comes to $1,165.50. A home inside Knoxville adds the city's rate on top, because county residents who live in the city pay both. The county page does not print the city rate, so ask the City of Knoxville for it.

Source: Knox County Finance, General Information page.

What dates matter on the Knox County tax calendar?

The Assessor's calendar page maps out the tax year. Current-year taxes become due on October 1, and the final day for payment with no penalty or interest is February 28. March 1 is the delinquency date for the prior year. Today is November 15, 2026, so a 2026 bill is open and payable through the last day of February 2027.

The assessment side runs on its own clock:

  • January 1 is the assessment date for ownership and condition
  • March 15 is the greenbelt application deadline
  • May 20 is the deadline to apply for exemptions, and assessment change notices should be mailed by then
  • June 1 starts the County Board of Equalization, which meets through June
  • August 1 is the general deadline for State Board appeals, or 45 days after the county board's notice, whichever comes later

Knox County runs a two-year reappraisal cycle. Year one is field work and sales data, and year two applies the valuation models and mails new values with instructions for appeal. The county says reappraisal does not automatically raise taxes, because the Commission may adjust the rate afterward. The Assessor also hosts a property tax calculator and a parcel lookup, so an owner can check a value before the notice arrives.

Does Knox County offer tax relief or a freeze?

Yes, through the Trustee. The 2026 senior freeze is for owners who will be 65 or older by December 31, 2026, with combined 2025 income for the owner, spouse and all deed owners under $63,470, and VA income counts. State tax relief is available for disabled veterans, up to $444 for 2026 with no income limit, and for widows and widowers of a disabled veteran who have not remarried.

Relief is a state-funded payment credit and not an exemption, so the bill still arrives and must be paid. The enrollment window for the 2026 tax year runs from October 1, 2026 through April 5, 2027. The Trustee says the state sets that window, the county cannot change it, and no extensions are given. Applications cannot be accepted by email, but a form can be requested at taxrelief@knoxcounty.org or by calling 865-215-8554 for the recorded information line.

What is Knox County itself like?

Knox County was created on June 11, 1792, and covers 526 square miles, 508 of them land. It sits in the Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians, with long ridges such as Bays Mountain and Sharp's Ridge running northeast to southwest, and House Mountain at 2,064 feet is the high point. The Holston and French Broad rivers meet in the east of the county to form the Tennessee River, and that stretch is part of Fort Loudoun Lake. Knoxville is the county seat, and the town of Farragut is also within the county.

Census Bureau QuickFacts shows a growing market:

  • 511,453 residents on July 1, 2025, up 6.8% since April 2020
  • 65.2% owner-occupied, with a median home value of $320,900 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $74,222 and 12.8% of people in poverty
  • Median monthly owner cost of $1,589 with a mortgage and median rent of $1,261

The county's property assessor's office, tax offices and Metropolitan Planning Commission are combined between city and county, which is why a Knoxville homeowner deals with the same Trustee and Assessor as a rural owner.

What happens to Knox County property tax when a house is sold?

The Assessor sends a sales questionnaire whenever ownership changes, including private sales and transfers into a trust or estate. Once the Register of Deeds has the new deed on record, the Assessor changes the owner's name, which can take up to a week, and anyone still seeing the old name after a month should call 865-215-2360. Closing agents ask the Trustee for the payoff on the current year's bill and for any delinquent years.

Mid-year changes to a property are prorated under Tennessee Code section 67-5-603. A fire, demolition or finished addition between January 1 and September 1 changes the assessed value for part of that year only. A seller who rebuilt or tore down a structure should ask for a field review so the bill matches the house being sold.

The Trustee's tax sale page shows what happens to accounts that stay unpaid. The most recent sale listed was June 2, 2026, at The Grande Event Center on Clinton Highway, run through the Clerk and Master, and bidders had to be current on their own taxes. That date has passed, and the Trustee posts the next one when the court sets it.

More questions about Knox County, TN Property Tax Guide

When are Knox County property taxes due?

Current-year taxes become due and payable on October 1, and the final day for payment with no penalty or interest is February 28. March 1 is the delinquency date for the prior year's taxes.

What is the Knox County property tax rate?

The county levy for fiscal 2026 is $1.5540 per $100 of assessed value. A home inside a city also owes that city's rate, which the county page does not list.

Where does a Knox County owner file an assessment appeal?

Go first to the county board, which starts meeting June 1, and then to the state board by August 1 or 45 days after the county notice was sent. Before either, the Assessor at 865-215-2360 can arrange a field review.

What is the deadline for the Knox County senior tax freeze?

April 5, 2027 for the 2026 tax year. Applicants must be 65 or older by December 31, 2026, with 2025 combined income under $63,470.

Can I sell a Knox County house that owes property tax?

Yes. The Trustee supplies a payoff figure, and the closing agent clears it out of what the seller receives. Accounts left unpaid for years can end up at a court-run tax sale.

Sumner County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Sumner County?

The Assessor of Property, John M. Hurt, sets values from Room 206 of the building at 355 N. Belvedere Drive in Gallatin (615-452-2412, open weekdays from 8:00 until 4:30). The office is on the second floor, just behind the Walmart. The Trustee, Cindy Williams, collects the tax from Room 107 in the same building (615-452-1260, on the same schedule).

Mailing changes for tax bills run through the assessor, whose edits to the roll feed the printed bills. A new owner who wants the notice mailed to a different address should call 615-452-2412 after closing.

Property tax sales are not run by either office. The assessor's FAQ sends people to the Clerk and Master for tax sale information.

What makes Sumner County's housing market different?

Sumner County lies on Tennessee's northern border, about 25 miles northeast of Nashville, and belongs to the Nashville metropolitan area. It covers 543 square miles, with the Cumberland River long the main route for trade. Gallatin holds the courthouse offices, and Hendersonville has the most people. Goodlettsville, Millersville, Mitchellville, Portland, Westmoreland and White House complete the eight cities, and several of them extend into neighboring counties.

Growth is the story here. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts show:

  • 215,538 residents in July 2025, up 9.8% from April 2020
  • 89,138 housing units, 72.0% owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied value of $393,100 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent of $1,424 and median household income of $90,301
  • 3,045 building permits in 2025, with 8.3% of residents in poverty

Schools are run by the Sumner County Board of Education, a twelve-member body with eleven elected district members and the Director of Schools. Because values here are higher than in Sullivan or Shelby, each point of tax rate matters more to a Sumner seller.

How is a Sumner County tax bill worked out?

The assessor lists four parts: appraised value, an assessment ratio set by state law, the assessed value, and the rate. Houses and farms are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value and commercial or industrial property at 40 percent. The county commission sets the county rate, and each city may add its own.

The calculation page posts these rates, each applied per hundred dollars of assessed value:

The county's own example is a $200,000 house: assessed value $50,000, which at the county rate gives $711. Call the assessor to confirm the rates for the current year before relying on these figures.

When and how do I pay Sumner County property tax?

Payment comes due the first Monday in October. A bill settled by February 28 has no interest, and March 1 begins delinquency. The Trustee accepts payment in these ways:

  • Online at tnpayments.com with Visa or Mastercard
  • By mail, with the top portion of the notice
  • In person at Room 107
  • By phone with a Visa or Mastercard
  • At local banks listed on the back of the notice

Cards cost 2.65 percent plus $1, a charge from the processing company. A taxpayer may split the bill into as many as five partial payments by check or cash, and whatever remains after February picks up interest on March 1. The paid status of a bill can be checked under the online payment link.

What is the path to contest a Sumner County valuation?

Call the assessor during the first week of May to book a hearing with the Sumner County Board of Equalization, which meets in June. An informal talk with the appraisal staff comes first and can be skipped. Compare your house with nearby sales and note any zoning or physical changes before you call.

The state's calendar sets May 20 as the date by which change notices should be mailed and exemptions applied for. A further appeal to the State Board of Equalization is due by August 1 or 45 days after the county board's notice, so for 2026 only owners with a later notice can still file. The assessor says values normally stay put between reappraisals, and the county is on a five-year cycle with the next one in 2029. Staff visit every property's exterior in between.

What relief and freeze programs does Sumner County run?

The Trustee runs the state tax relief rebate for elderly, disabled and disabled veteran owners, and a freeze for the county and some Sumner cities. Freeze applications for 2026 open in September 2026, relief applications are taken when bills go out, and the deadline is 35 days after the February payment date. Seniors 65 and over qualify on income. For disabled veterans and their widows, the programs are not income based. Everyone must requalify every year.

Appointments can be made by phone at 615-452-1260 or through the Trustee's online scheduler.

What does a house inside a Sumner County city pay?

An address inside a city limit owes the county rate plus the city rate. Using the posted figures on the same $200,000 house, a Gallatin address adds about $264.75 to the county's $711, for roughly $975.75. A Hendersonville address adds about $294.15, for roughly $1,005.15. These are illustrations of the arithmetic only, and cities may also levy special assessments, which the assessor says to ask each city about.

A rural address outside every city pays the county rate alone. That difference is worth checking on a listing, since two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills.

Which other Sumner County deadlines can affect a seller?

Which Blount County offices handle property tax?

Three bodies split the work. The Property Assessor values every parcel, the Blount County Board of Commissioners sets the tax rate, and the Trustee collects the money. The Assessor's office is at 351 Court Street in the Blount County Courthouse, Maryville, TN 37804, phone 865-273-5850, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Trustee is on the third floor of the courthouse at 347 Court Street, phone 865-273-5900, with the same hours.

The county's assessor page says the office must appraise and assess about 70,000 parcels and audit at least 10 percent of business personal property accounts each year. It also makes the point that the assessor does not raise or lower taxes, since the amount owed comes from the assessed value multiplied by the tax rate. The Trustee's property tax page adds that the Trustee does not set rates or appraisals and only collects.

Blount County includes the cities of Maryville, Alcoa, Townsend, Friendsville and Rockford, plus the town of Louisville and part of Vonore. The county page covers county tax. A city may bill its own tax, and the Tennessee Comptroller notes that a city collector can be the city treasurer, the city recorder or the county trustee, so ask the city about any separate bill.

What is Blount County like, and why does it matter for a tax bill?

Blount County covers 567 square miles in East Tennessee, with Maryville as the county seat and largest city. The southern part rises into the Great Smoky Mountains, where the crest forms the border with North Carolina and Thunderhead Mountain reaches 5,527 feet. The northern part is Ridge-and-Valley country, and the Tennessee River forms part of the line with Knox County through Fort Loudoun Lake. Cades Cove is one of the most visited sections of the national park.

Schools affect where a home sits in the county's market. Blount County Schools serves the county except inside the cities of Maryville and Alcoa, which run their own school systems. Maryville College, founded in 1819, is downtown, and Denso Manufacturing Tennessee is the county's largest employer, with about 3,000 workers.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Blount County:

  • 143,820 residents in July 2025, up 6.3% from April 2020
  • 64,682 housing units, with 77.0% owner-occupied
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes of $320,500 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $77,365 and 9.2% of people in poverty
  • 790 building permits in 2025

How is a Blount County property tax bill calculated?

The bill equals the appraised value, times the assessment percentage for the property type, times the tax rate per $100 of assessed value. The assessor page lists the percentages:

  • Residential improvements and residential land: 25 percent of fair market value (land may be assessed on market value or use value)
  • Commercial property: 40 percent of fair market value
  • Personal property of commercial businesses: 30 percent of the appraised value reported on the Tangible Personal Property Schedule

The county's own example uses a $250,000 residential property. At 25 percent the assessment is $62,500, and at the 2026 rate of $1.29 per $100 the county tax bill is $806. Rates for earlier years were $2.47 per $100 from 2015 through 2022, $1.59 from 2023 through 2025, and $1.29 for 2026.

The Trustee reports where the money goes: 46.50 percent to general county purposes, 42.65 percent to education and 10.85 percent to debt, with over 95 percent of that debt tied to education. Property tax is about 40 percent of the funds the Trustee collects, and State of Tennessee money, mainly for education, is another 30 percent.

When is Blount County property tax due, and what discount applies now?

County notices are typically mailed in early to mid-September and payable through the end of February. Taxes become delinquent on March 1, and state law adds 1.5 percent interest per month to delinquent property tax until it is paid. The county gives a 2 percent discount for payment by the end of October and 1 percent during November. Today is November 15, 2026, so the 1 percent discount is still open through November 30 and the 2 percent discount has ended.

State law does not require a notice, and the county sends one as a reminder. An owner who has not received one by October 1 should call the Trustee. Payment options include:

  • In person or by mail at 347 Court Street, Maryville
  • Online by card or e-check, and by phone at 855-777-3468, with a convenience fee that goes to the payment vendors and not to the county
  • Most Blount County banks until the delinquency date, with the tax notice in hand, though state law does not allow payment at credit unions

How do I appeal a Blount County assessment?

Start with the County Board of Equalization, which meets June 1. A disputed assessment must first go to the county board or it becomes final, with limited exceptions. Some assessors offer an informal review, which can speed a correction, though it does not count as an appeal. Contact the Assessor at 865-273-5850 to ask whether Blount County does and how to get on the county board's schedule.

An owner who disagrees with the county board's decision can appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. For tax year 2026 the August 1 date has passed, so an owner with a later notice should call the State Board at 615-401-7883 to check the 45-day window. The state hearing is held before an administrative judge, who must issue a ruling within 90 days. The taxpayer carries the burden of proof.

The state's guidance points to evidence that works:

  • Sales of comparable properties, with differences in size, age, condition and location explained
  • An appraisal, which may be presented and may require the appraiser to testify
  • A statement of the value the owner claims, since a bare claim of overvaluation is generally not enough

Pay at least the undisputed part of the bill before it goes delinquent. Any delinquent taxes from earlier years must be paid in full as well, and the Comptroller's appeal page explains how to work out the undisputed amount. A higher value after a countywide reappraisal does not by itself show the assessment is wrong.

What tax relief and freeze programs does Blount County offer?

Two state programs run through the Trustee's office. The Property Tax Relief Program is a rebate for homeowners 65 or older whose combined income from all sources for all owners, spouse included, is not over $38,470, using 2025 income for the 2026 tax year. It can also reach totally and permanently disabled taxpayers with the same income limit, certain service-connected disabled veterans and certain widows of those veterans.

The Property Tax Freeze Program lets owners 65 or older by the end of the tax year freeze all or part of their county tax. They must be the owners on the recorded deed, live in the home as a principal residence and have 2025 combined income of no more than $63,470. State law limits how much land qualifies, so a 100-acre farm would freeze only the residence and part of its land. Owners must apply and be approved every year.

The deadline for both programs for the 2026 tax year is April 5, 2027. Call 865-273-5900 to learn what documents are needed.

What happens to property tax when a Blount County house is sold?

The official tax roll reflects ownership on January 1, so the name on the 2026 bill may be the seller's even after a fall closing. The Trustee says taxes are normally prorated at closing and the buyer becomes responsible, and that its office tries to send the notice to the new owner but does not always know who agreed to pay. A buyer who gets no notice should call the Trustee and ask for the status of the parcel.

A seller who owes back tax should check the amount with the Trustee early. Interest of 1.5 percent a month runs on delinquent taxes. A seller who needs a quick closing and has an unpaid balance, a pending appeal or an estate to settle can ask the title company how those items will be handled at the table.

What is the Blount County property tax rate for 2026?

The 2026 county rate is $1.29 per $100 of assessed value, set by the Blount County Board of Commissioners. On a $250,000 home assessed at 25 percent, the county's example works out to $806. Any city tax would be separate.

When are Blount County property taxes delinquent?

They become delinquent on March 1, after the payment period that runs through the end of February. State law adds 1.5 percent interest each month to delinquent property tax. The 2026 deadline for relief and freeze applications is April 5, 2027.

Is there still a discount for paying Blount County property tax early?

Yes, for a short time. The 2 percent discount ended with October, and the 1 percent discount applies to payments made during November. Discounts are shown on the tax notice and are not available after those periods.

Where do I pay property tax in Blount County?

Pay the Trustee at 347 Court Street, Maryville, by mail, online, or by phone at 855-777-3468. Most Blount County banks accept payment until the delinquency date, but credit unions cannot take payments under state law. Card and e-check payments carry a convenience fee.

How do I challenge my Blount County property value?

File a complaint with the County Board of Equalization, which meets June 1, then appeal to the State Board of Equalization if needed. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal. Pay at least the undisputed part of the tax so the bill is not treated as delinquent.

Inside Bristol, Kingsport or Bluff City, a house may also receive a city bill, as the Trustee's FAQ explains. Ask the city about its own rate and due date.

How does Blountville's county compare in size and housing?

Sullivan County fills the northeast corner of Tennessee along the Virginia line. It was cut from Washington County in 1779 and covers 430 square miles, of which 413 are land. Kingsport has the most residents, and Bristol, Bluff City and a slice of Johnson City also fall inside. Blountville, the county seat, is the only unincorporated county seat in Tennessee.

The land runs from Ridge-and-Valley ridges in the west to the Blue Ridge in the east, where Holston Mountain tops out at 4,284 feet. The signed voucher must come back to a Trustee office each year by April 5, and bank branches do not accept it. Sullivan County does not offer a tax freeze program.

The Assessor's office also manages Greenbelt and Forestry assessments. The state calendar sets March 15 as the greenbelt application deadline and May 20 for exemption applications. An owner of acreage should call the Assessor about both programs before listing.

Whoever held title on January 1 gets the notice, even when the house changes hands later in the year. The Trustee says new owners still must see that the tax is paid on time, and to follow the settlement statement for the split. If a lender escrows the taxes, the mortgage company gets the bill.

The 2020 census counted 147,737 people and 58,152 housing units, and 75.1% of occupied homes were owner occupied. The 2025 estimate is 175,033, so assessments here reflect fast growth. Wilson County Schools runs 22 public schools, and the Lebanon Special School District serves most of Lebanon for grades K to 8.

When do Wilson County property taxes come due?

Tax notices go out in mid-October to the property address. The tax year runs January 1 through December 31, and the bill can be paid without interest from mid-October through the last day of February of the following year.

The assessment calendar shows where that bill comes from. The Assessor delivers the roll to the Trustee before the first Monday in October, and taxes become payable then. For the 2026 bills now in mailboxes, the no-interest window closes at the end of February 2027.

How can I pay a Wilson County tax bill?

The Trustee accepts several payment routes, and each has its own cost. Write the tax bill number on any check, or include the top portion of the notice.

  • By mail, with a check payable to Kenneth Hackett, Wilson County Trustee, sent to P.O. Box 865, Lebanon, TN 37088.
  • In person at 228 E Main Street, Room 102, Lebanon.
  • Online through the Tennessee Payments Portal by card or e-check. Cards carry a 2.50% fee, and the county notes the fee goes to the processor, not the Trustee.
  • By phone at 1-888-382-8422.
  • At Wilson Bank & Trust and Pinnacle Bank branches in Wilson County from October through February, with the bill in hand. Banks do not take partial payments.

If your lender escrows taxes, the statement you receive is a copy for your records, and the lender pays from the escrow account.

How do I appeal a Wilson County assessment?

Start with the Assessor's office, because a phone call or visit often clears a clerical error. If the answer does not satisfy you, the next step is the County Board of Equalization, which begins meeting June 1 each year.

That board has five property owners serving two year terms: one from Lebanon, one from Mt. Juliet and three from the county at large. The Assessor publishes a newspaper notice about ten days before it convenes, and appointments are usually made by phone or in person in the last week of May or the first week of June. Owners may appear themselves or send a family member, attorney or authorized agent, and should arrive about fifteen minutes early to fill out a form.

The board looks only at fair and equitable value. Evidence about how much tax you can afford does not help. Results are normally mailed before the end of June, and the decision letter explains how to go to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or 45 days after the letter, whichever is later.

What tax relief and freeze programs does Wilson County offer?

The Trustee runs two state and county programs. Tax Relief helps taxpayers 65 or older, disabled citizens, and total and permanent disabled veterans. The Tax Freeze program holds the tax amount on the primary residence of seniors 65 and older.

The county commission raised the freeze income limit for tax year 2026 from $51,790 to $63,470. Applicants meet with Trustee staff, and the process is explained on the back of the bill. They typically bring the prior year's tax return, a driver's license, and Social Security and Medicare cards, and the rules cover everyone listed on the deed. A frozen amount lasts until the next tax year, when the owner must reapply.

If you plan to sell, remember that the freeze applies to the owner's primary residence. Talk to the Trustee at option 2 on 615-444-0894 about what changes after a sale.

What should a Wilson County seller check about taxes before closing?

A few questions to settle before the contract date will keep the closing statement accurate.

  • Ask the Trustee for the current balance on the parcel and whether prior years show anything owed.
  • Confirm whether the property sits inside Lebanon or Watertown, whose city councils set their own property tax rates.
  • Ask the Assessor if any change notice or appeal is pending.
  • Find out whether a freeze or relief enrollment is on file under your name.
  • Tell the title company which tax year is unpaid so it can collect from your proceeds.

Business tangible personal property is a separate account. If a home business operated from the property, the schedule is due to the Assessor by March 1 each year, and the county places a forced assessment when none is filed.

Where do I pay property taxes in Wilson County, Tennessee?

Pay the Wilson County Trustee at 228 E Main Street, Room 102, Lebanon, by mail, online, by phone at 1-888-382-8422, or at participating bank branches from October through February. The Trustee's phone is 615-444-0894.

When are Wilson County property taxes late?

Taxes can be paid without interest from mid-October through the last day of February of the next year. The tax year itself runs January 1 through December 31. Ask the Trustee about the exact interest schedule after February.

How do I contest my Wilson County property value?

Call or visit the Assessor at 615-444-8661 first. If that does not settle it, request a hearing before the County Board of Equalization, which starts meeting June 1. A State Board of Equalization appeal is due by August 1 or 45 days after the county letter.

Does Wilson County offer a property tax freeze for seniors?

Yes. The Tax Freeze program fixes the tax on the primary residence of owners 65 and older who meet the income limit, which is $63,470 for tax year 2026. Applications go through the Trustee's office.

Who sets the property tax rate in Wilson County?

The County Commission sets the county rate, and the city councils of Lebanon and Watertown set their own city rates. The calendar places this in early July, August or September.

What is Maury County like, and who is buying here?

Maury County is in Middle Tennessee, south of Nashville, and has been growing quickly. Columbia holds the courthouse, and Spring Hill, which straddles the Williamson County line, is the biggest city. The county dates to 1807, when it was carved from Williamson County and Native lands. It covers 616 square miles and borders Williamson, Marshall, Giles, Lawrence, Lewis and Hickman counties. Its farmland made it a leader in beef cattle production, and James K. Polk's home in Columbia is a state historic site.

Roads explain a lot of the growth. Interstate 65 runs through the eastern part of the county for about 18 miles, State Route 396 links it to Spring Hill, and US 31 runs through both Columbia and Spring Hill. The Natchez Trace Parkway and the Duck River complex add outdoor space. Maury County Public Schools operates the public schools countywide.

How does the 2026 reappraisal affect a Maury County tax bill?

Maury County reappraises every four years, and 2026 is the current reappraisal year. The appraisal on file reflects market value on the first of January in the reappraisal year, with later improvements added at equalized value. With prices climbing across the county, an owner whose house was last valued before the recent run-up should look at the new notice closely.

The formula is short. Multiply the appraised value by the assessment ratio for the property's class, then apply the rate to every $100 of the result. Tennessee assesses residential property at 25 percent of appraised value. A house appraised at $355,700, equal to the county's median owner-occupied value, would carry an assessed value of $88,925 before any rate is applied.

The county's 2025 to 2026 budget letter to the state Comptroller reports that the Commission passed a rate of $1.91 for each $100 of assessment, with no increase for residents. A reappraisal year can lead to a different adopted rate, so ask the Trustee which rate is on your current bill. The Assessor's page explains the calculation and links to reappraisal guides.

The window opened in early October and closes at the end of February, so a Maury County owner can pay today, November 15, 2026, with no charge. The Trustee says all property taxes are due on receipt. On March 1 a penalty and interest charge of 1.5 percent begins and grows each month. Unpaid accounts move to Chancery Court on April 1.

The Trustee accepts partial payments, though interest applies to whatever is unpaid on March 1. A postmark counts as the payment date except when delinquent accounts move to Chancery Court. Since August 1, 2026 has passed, an owner holding a late county notice should count forward from the mailing date. An administrative judge hears the case and rules no more than 90 days after the hearing, and court review has to be sought inside 60 days once the state board's order is final.

Some assessors offer an informal review that can speed a correction. It is no appeal and protects nothing later, so ask whether the Maury office offers one and still file with the county board to keep every option.

Is tax relief available to Maury County homeowners?

Yes. The Trustee's office helps elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans apply for the Tennessee Tax Relief Program under state guidelines. Call 931-375-2201 for the forms and the current income limits.

The Trustee also offers ACH debits that can spread the bill into equal monthly payments. Call 931-375-2201 to ask how to enroll.

How does a sale change who pays Maury County tax?

The tax year runs on the calendar, and the notice goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. A sale in the fall therefore leaves the seller's name on the bill even though the buyer will carry the house into the next year. Request the Trustee's exact balance and let the title agent split it at closing.

Late sellers face a short clock, because charges start in March and the Chancery Court turnover follows in April. Any balance still open at closing comes out of the seller's net, so confirm the amount with the Trustee a week ahead.

On March 1. Interest of 1.5 percent a month starts then and climbs each month, and on April 1 the county turns delinquent accounts over to Chancery Court. Payment is open from the first Monday in October through February.

Yes, the Trustee accepts them. Interest still applies on March 1 to any balance left unpaid, so a partial payment lowers the amount that accrues interest without ending it.

A house inside Cleveland gets two bills, one from the county and one from the city. The city's tax page says so directly. A house in Bradley County outside any city gets the county bill only.

How is a Bradley County property tax bill calculated?

Tennessee multiplies the appraised value by an assessment ratio, then applies the tax rate per $100 of assessed value. The Comptroller lists the ratio at 25 percent for residential and farm property and 40 percent for commercial and industrial property.

Bradley County's 2026 net property tax rate is $1.0772 per $100 of assessed value. County-only properties in the fire service district pay an extra $0.2558, for a combined $1.3330.   • Timing: new applicants for tax relief and tax freeze sign up from October 1, 2026 through April 5, 2027.

Taxes stay with the property. The county's FAQ says that if the deed changes after January 1, the bill still goes to the owner of record as of that date, and the new owner can ask for a copy. Unpaid taxes keep accruing against the parcel.

The closing statement should show how the year's tax was split. Bradley County tells new owners to check with the title company or review the closing statement to see how it was settled. If taxes go unpaid long enough, the Clerk and Master can sell the parcel at auction. Cleveland's page adds that city delinquent taxes go to the Clerk and Master after 12 months of penalty.

Bradley County had an estimated 115,465 residents in July 2025, with 67.3 percent of homes owner-occupied and a median household income of $66,552. Who bills and collects property tax in Hawkins County, Tennessee?

Two offices in the Rogersville courthouse annex split the work. The Hawkins County Property Assessor sets the value, and the Hawkins County Trustee turns that value and the commission's rate into a bill and collects it. Tax bills usually go out after the County Commission sets the rate and passes the budget, normally no later than October 15.

The Trustee is Jim Shanks, first elected in 2014. His office is at 110 East Main Street, Room 203, Rogersville, TN 37857, phone (423) 272-7022. The Assessor is Michael S. Gillespie at 110 East Main Street, Room 201, phone (423) 272-8505. Both offices close at four in the afternoon on weekdays and open at eight, and the Trustee also closes for lunch from noon to one.

When is Hawkins County property tax due and what does late payment cost?

Taxes can be paid without interest from October 1 through the end of February. Starting March 1, interest of 1.5% a month is added, so a $2,000 bill grows by $30 for each month it stays open.

The Trustee accepts partial payments, but the owner must sign a form each tax year before the first partial payment is taken. Cash, check, money order and debit or credit cards (Mastercard or Visa) are accepted. A card payment carries a 2.65% processing fee plus a $1.00 convenience fee. A satellite office at 150 South Central in Church Hill, phone (423) 357-4350, opens for the season from mid-October to mid-March. How is a Hawkins County tax bill figured?

The Assessor supplies the assessed value, the County Commission sets the rate, and the Trustee multiplies the two to produce the bill. The Trustee's page includes a tax calculator if you want to test a figure before the bills arrive.

Hawkins County's commission has 14 members, two from each of seven civil districts, and it adopts the rate along with the annual budget for the general, school and highway funds. A higher rate is a public decision with notices and hearings, so the commission's budget meetings before bills go out are the time to speak. The largest private employers listed in a 2018 state profile included BAE Systems, AGC Flat Glass and Barrette Outdoor Living.

What is the appeal route for a Hawkins County assessment?

Start with the Assessor's office at (423) 272-8505 and ask for an informal review. Bring proof that the value is too high, such as sales of similar homes or an appraisal. If the review does not settle it, file with the Hawkins County Board of Equalization, then with the State Board of Equalization. The Assessor's page warns that deadlines are strictly enforced.

This year's county board hearings ran from June 1 through June 26, 2026, so that window has closed for tax year 2026. Assessment change notices go out in May, and the county board starts meeting again each June. Watch your mail in spring, since a notice is sent only when a value changed.

  • If the County Commission adopts a higher rate than the certified one, that counts as a tax increase and needs public notice and hearings.

What tax relief is available to Hawkins County homeowners?

The state runs a relief program for elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans, and the Hawkins County Trustee takes the applications. Income counts, and proof of income is required. The application must be completed no later than April 4 after the February 28 payment deadline.

Tax relief is a reimbursement from the state toward taxes already owed, not an exemption, according to the Tennessee Comptroller. You still receive a bill and must pay it. Relief covers only your primary residence, and the amount changes with your assessment and tax rate. The statutes are Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-701 through 67-5-704.

Farm and forest owners can ask about greenbelt. The application is due March 15, and the Assessor notes that once land stops qualifying, a roll-back tax equal to the taxes saved over the last three years comes due.

What happens to unpaid Hawkins County taxes if I sell?

Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel, so the title company needs a current payoff from the Trustee before closing. Ask the Trustee for the balance through your expected closing date, including any March-onward interest.

Taxes that stay unpaid are collected through the Hawkins County Chancery Court. The Clerk and Master, Brent Price, collects delinquent property taxes for the county and the towns. His office is at 100 E. Main Street, Suite 316, Rogersville, and the number for delinquent tax questions is (423) 272-8150. The Clerk and Master's page lists a delinquent tax sale list dated November 17, 2026, and offers online delinquent tax payments, searchable by parcel number. The same page notes that probate matters in this court require an attorney under local rules.

If you are behind, call the Clerk and Master and ask where your parcel stands on that list.

What is Hawkins County like for homeowners and sellers?

Hawkins County covers about 500 square miles in the northeast corner of Tennessee, with Rogersville as the county seat and its 1836 courthouse the oldest in the state. Church Hill is the largest city. Bulls Gap, Mount Carmel and Surgoinsville are towns, and Bean Station and Kingsport reach into the county.

The Census Bureau estimates 59,559 residents for 2025 and about 28,006 housing units. For 2020-2024 it reports 80.1% owner-occupied homes, a median owner-occupied value of $176,300, median gross rent of $785 and a median household income of $56,936. Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage are $1,136.

  • The county government does not issue building permits and has no zoning restrictions or code enforcement, according to the county home page. Permits come through the State of Tennessee.
  • Septic records, if you need them for a sale, come from the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation. You may need the name of the original owner.
  • New 911 address questions go to (423) 272-7532.
  • School districts serving the county are Hawkins County, Kingsport City and Rogersville City, which covers elementary grades only.

Pay the Hawkins County Trustee at 110 East Main Street, Room 203, Rogersville, or at the Church Hill office from mid-October to mid-March. Online payment is linked from the county home page. Card payments add a 2.65% fee plus $1.00.

When do Hawkins County property taxes become delinquent?

Delinquency begins once February ends. Interest of 1.5% per month is added from March 1. The Trustee accepts partial payments if the owner signs the required form for that tax year.

Michael S. Gillespie is the Assessor. The office is at 110 East Main Street, Room 201, Rogersville, and the phone number is (423) 272-8505. The office opens at eight and closes at four on weekdays.

Is the 2026 appeal window still open in Hawkins County?

No. County Board of Equalization hearings ran June 1 through June 26, 2026. The county board starts meeting again in June, and the Assessor's office handles informal reviews first.

Who handles delinquent tax sales in Hawkins County?

The Chancery Court Clerk and Master handles them. Call (423) 272-8150 for delinquent tax questions. The office has posted a delinquent tax sale list dated November 17, 2026.

Montgomery County by the numbers

Which offices bill and value property in Montgomery County?

Look for Veterans Plaza, 350 Pageant Lane, Clarksville. The Assessor of Property occupies Suite 101-C and values every parcel. The County Trustee is in Suite 101-B and issues the bills.

  • Assessor of Property Erinne Hester: 931-648-5709, counter hours 8 to 4:30 on weekdays.
  • County Trustee: 931-648-5717, weekdays from half past seven until 4:30.
  • Delinquent tax suits: Clerk and Master of the Montgomery Chancery Court, 2 Millennium Plaza, Suite 101, 931-648-5703.

County commissioners adopt the rate, and the Trustee applies it per $100 of assessed value. A house within Clarksville limits gets a second bill from the City of Clarksville, so a seller there clears two balances.

What kind of county is Montgomery County for a seller?

The county was formed in 1796. Clarksville is its seat and its single incorporated municipality, and the county belongs to the Clarksville, TN-KY metro area. QuickFacts shows 249,935 residents in July 2025, up 13.6% from 220,012 at the 2020 base.

Other Census figures describe a growing, mostly owned housing stock.

  • 102,547 housing units as of July 2025.
  • 61.9% of homes occupied by their owners, 2020 to 2024.
  • $280,200 as the typical owner-occupied home value.
  • $75,613 in median household income, and $1,308 in median gross rent.
  • 30,166 resident veterans.

Land area is 539 square miles, roughly 408 residents per square mile, and workers average 27.8 minutes to get to a job. At the median value and the 25% residential ratio, assessed value comes to $70,050, which is the figure the sample bill below uses.

What are the 2026 tax rates and how is a Montgomery County bill calculated?

The Trustee's FAQ gives the 2026 county rate as $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville's FAQ lists the city rate as $1.01. A property inside the city therefore carries a combined $3.11 per $100.

Assessed value is a share of appraised value that depends on use: residential and farm are 25%, commercial and industrial 40%, personal property 30%, and public utilities 55%. The Trustee's method is to multiply the appraisal by the class percentage, divide by 100, then multiply by the rate.

What are the payment dates and late charges on a Montgomery County bill?

Bills are mailed during the final week of October. The window opens the first Monday in October and closes on the last day of February with no interest. After that, each month from March 1 adds 1.5 percent to the base tax, an annual 18 percent.

State law does not make the Trustee mail notices, and the county says a bill that never arrived is no defense for lateness. Partial payments toward the current year start July 10, as long as the balance is paid by the February cutoff. A payment mailed through the Postal Service counts on its postmark date, but office meter stamps do not count.

Online e-checks carry a 1.75 percent plus $1 charge, and Visa or MasterCard payments carry 2.65 percent plus $1. Cash works only at the counter. Several local banks accept current-year payments through February 28 when you show the original bill or a copy from the Trustee's website.

Clarksville adds its own steps for city tax. After a full year of delinquency the city passes the account to its delinquent tax attorney, and later payments go to the Clerk and Master at the chancery court.

What is the path for contesting a Montgomery County valuation?

Phone the Assessor at 931-648-5709 before anything else. A wrong room count or land class is often settled in one call. Unresolved disputes go to the county equalization board, which starts its June session on the first business day of the month and continues until its docket is finished.

To get a time slot, call the Assessor between May 15 and May 31. Five property owners from around the county make up the board, and state law reserves two seats for Clarksville residents. You can appear yourself or send a relative, lawyer or authorized agent. Bring appraisals, repair bills and comparable assessments. Leave out talk of what you can afford, since the board weighs value only.

The decision letter normally arrives before July. If you still disagree, the State Board of Equalization takes the next appeal, which must reach it by August 1 or 45 days after the county mailing, whichever falls later. The Assessor lists 2029 as the year of the next countywide reappraisal.

What tax relief and special bills affect a Montgomery County sale?

State relief repays a portion of the tax for low-income elderly and disabled owners and for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. The Comptroller describes it as reimbursement, so you still receive and pay the bill. Only a primary residence qualifies, and a house held in an irrevocable trust does not.

In Clarksville, the Trustee's office is where you sign up for the Tax Freeze program, and relief applications are available at both the county Trustee and the city Finance and Revenue Department. Approved owners get a voucher with each bill and must send it in every year to both offices.

Greenbelt land brings another charge. If a sale ends the farm, forest or open-space classification, rollback taxes for the previous three years (five for open space) come due, and unless the contract says otherwise the seller owes them. A buyer who promises to keep the classification has 90 days after the sale to file the form with the Assessor, or the rollback becomes the buyer's problem. Unpaid rollback tax is a first lien on the land either way.

How does Montgomery County tax get settled at a closing?

New owners are told by the Trustee to check the closing statement or ask the title company who owes the year's tax. The lien-like effect is the key point: unpaid tax keeps accruing against the house whatever the purchase contract says. Clarksville's FAQ goes further and warns that a delinquent property can still end up at a tax auction.

Request a balance from the Trustee for county tax and from city Finance and Revenue for city tax. Find out whether your lender already paid from escrow, because the city refunds a double payment to whoever paid last. Then have the title company pay any remaining balance out of the seller's proceeds.

What are the 2026 property tax rates in Montgomery County?

The county charges $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville charges $1.01 on top of that inside city limits. A residential parcel is assessed at 25 percent of its appraised value.

What is the deadline to pay Montgomery County tax without interest?

The last day of February. The window opens on the first Monday of October. From March 1, 1.5 percent a month is added to the base tax.

Where do I start if my Montgomery County valuation looks too high?

Call the Assessor at 931-648-5709. If that fails, book a June hearing with the County Board of Equalization between May 15 and June 1, and use the State Board of Equalization after that.

Does a Clarksville house owe both city and county tax?

Yes. The Trustee collects only the county share, and the city bills its own. Homes outside the city limits owe the county portion alone.

Who owes the tax when a Montgomery County house sells?

The sale contract and the closing statement settle that between buyer and seller. The tax follows the calendar year and the property itself, so the title company should confirm the split and clear any balance at closing.

Who handles property tax in Roane County?

Three courthouse offices touch a Roane County tax bill, and all sit at 200 E. Race Street in Kingston. The Assessor of Property values the land, the Trustee collects the money, and the Clerk and Master takes over if the bill goes unpaid long enough to reach court.

  • Assessor of Property, Suite 5, 865-376-4362: values, ownership updates, greenbelt and tax freeze paperwork

The Trustee's page states that the Trustee does not set the rate or the appraisal. That is a common point of confusion. If you disagree with a value, you go to the Assessor and the county Board of Equalization. If you disagree with a rate, note that the assessor's page puts rate setting with the County Commission.

When are Roane County property taxes due?

Taxes are due to the Trustee on October 1, according to the Assessor's calendar. The Trustee says notices normally go out in late September and the tax is payable through the end of February. The bill becomes delinquent on March 1.

Many owners wait until winter, and that is allowed. If the house is for sale, though, an unpaid bill from the current year shows up in the title search and gets paid at closing. A seller who pays in the fall removes one item from the settlement statement.

Where can you pay? The Trustee lists three routes. Online payment carries a convenience fee that the county does not keep. United Community Bank in Kingston and SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman take payments with no fee. The office also accepts partial payments when you pay in person.

How do assessments and appeals work in Roane County?

The Assessor values property as of January 1 and works on a four-year reappraisal cycle. Roane County's most recent reappraisal was the 2025 cycle. Values stay put between cycles unless the property changes physically, so a sale alone does not reset the number.

  • January 1: assessment date for ownership, assessments and tax maps
  • March 15: deadline to apply for greenbelt on land of 15 acres or more used for agriculture or forestry
  • May: assessment change notices go to owners whose appraisal changed
  • June 1: the County Board of Equalization begins hearing appeals
  • October 1: taxes are due to the Trustee

If your notice looks too high, call the Assessor at 865-376-4362 first and ask what comparable sales support the number. Take that to the Board of Equalization if the talk does not resolve it. Ask the office for the current filing deadline, because the board's schedule changes by year.

What tax relief and greenbelt options exist in Roane County?

Roane County offers three tools, each run through a different counter.

  • State tax relief for homeowners 65 or older, homeowners who are 100 percent disabled, certain service-connected disabled veterans and spouses of veterans killed in action. The Trustee handles the paperwork, the state decides eligibility, and the income limit changes each year.
  • The property tax freeze, adopted by the County Commission in 2007 under a state program. It is open to homeowners 65 or older under a state income limit, with no more than 5 acres, and the Trustee takes the annual application.
  • Greenbelt, filed with the Assessor by March 15, for farm or forest tracts of 15 acres or more.

Greenbelt carries a price on exit. When land stops qualifying, a roll-back charge equal to the taxes saved over the last three years comes due. A buyer or seller of a farm parcel should ask the Assessor whether greenbelt status is attached before a contract is signed.

What happens to delinquent Roane County taxes?

The Trustee's page says delinquent bills stay in its office for 18 months before they pass to the Clerk and Master. The delinquent tax page says a Chancery Court suit follows in March of the next year, with filing fees added and monthly interest still running. Ask both offices which one holds your year. Once the suit is filed, you pay the Clerk and Master and not the Trustee, and partial payments for a tax year are refused.

You can stop a sale by paying everything owed before the sale begins. The Clerk and Master asks for the map, group and parcel number and takes a business or cashier's check, a call to 865-376-2487, or an in-person payment. Call for a total, because interest adds on every month.

The county holds a back tax sale once a year at the courthouse. The next one is set for March 6, 2027. Property sells as is, bidders must be 18 or older and registered before the sale, and the court must confirm each sale. The usual redemption period is one year from the confirming order. For properties sold at the March 2027 sale where taxes are more than three years delinquent, a law effective July 1, 2026 cuts that to 90 days.

How do you sell a Roane County house with tax due?

Get a payoff, and pay it from the sale. The Trustee gives the figure while the bill is in its office, and the Clerk and Master gives it after a lawsuit.

  • Ask which office holds each year, since the answer decides where the check goes.
  • Give the closing agent the map, group and parcel number from your tax bill.
  • If you owe more than one year, request a total as of your closing date.
  • A city lot in Harriman, Kingston, Rockwood, Oak Ridge or Oliver Springs can carry a city charge as well, and the Clerk and Master collects delinquent city taxes too.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can close on a short timeline when the payoff is clean. That helps when a tax sale date is approaching.

What does Roane County look like for a seller?

Roane County covers 395 square miles, with 361 of land. Kingston is the county seat and Oak Ridge is the largest city. Harriman, Rockwood and Oliver Springs are the other incorporated places, and Midtown is a census-designated place. The Tennessee, Clinch and Emory rivers run through the county, mostly as Watts Bar Lake, and Walden Ridge rises on the Cumberland Plateau side.

The county was formed in 1801 and named for Archibald Roane, the second governor of Tennessee. Kingston is rooted in Fort Southwest Point, a frontier fort of the early 1790s. Rockwood became an iron and coal center, and Harriman was planned as a temperance town. Oak Ridge began in World War II as a Manhattan Project city, and the K-25 plant and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are in the county.

The Census Bureau counts 57,395 people on July 1, 2025, up 7.2 percent from the 2020 base. It lists 26,696 housing units and a 78.1 percent owner-occupancy rate. Median household income is $71,885, median rent is $785, and 24.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. That is the oldest population of the four Tennessee counties in the Census comparison table. The county issued 380 building permits in 2025.

When are Roane County property taxes due?

October 1 is the due date on the Assessor's calendar, and the tax is payable through the end of February. Unpaid bills become delinquent on March 1.

What is the 2026 Roane County property tax rate?

The county rate is $1.4523 per $100 of assessed value for city residents and $1.4987 outside the cities. City rates add to the county rate: Rockwood $0.6265, Harriman $0.7024, Kingston $0.8234, Oliver Springs $0.92 and Oak Ridge $1.3784.

Where can I pay Roane County property tax in person?

At the Trustee's office in the Courthouse, 200 E. Race Street, Suite 4, Kingston, or at United Community Bank in Kingston or SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman, where no fee is charged. Online payments carry a convenience fee.

When is the next Roane County tax sale?

The Clerk and Master lists the next Back Tax Sale for March 6, 2027. You can pay delinquent taxes up to the day of the sale, before it begins, to take a parcel off the list.

Can I freeze my Roane County property tax?

Possibly. Homeowners 65 or older with income under the state limit and no more than 5 acres can apply to the Trustee for the tax freeze each year. Call 865-376-4938 for the form and the current limit.

Carter County by the numbers

Who collects property tax in Carter County, Tennessee?

The Carter County Trustee collects county property taxes at the Carter County Courthouse, 801 East Elk Avenue, Elizabethton, TN 37643. The courthouse main number is 423-542-1801, and the Trustee's page lists 423-542-1811 for delinquent tax questions.

The Trustee page says taxes can be searched and paid on citisenportal.com, either with an account or as a guest. An account sends email notices about future bills. To change a billing address, the page tells owners to contact the Assessor of Property, not the Trustee.

Property inside Elizabethton owes two taxes, one to the county and one to the city. The city's own announcement states that property in the corporate limits is subject to both. Rural parcels in Carter County outside the city pay the county bill only.

Who sets the value of a Carter County house?

The Assessor of Property, Shane Simerly, appraises every parcel. The office is in the courthouse, the phone is 423-542-1801, and email goes to assessor@cartercountytn.gov. The county site links a real estate assessment data search for looking up a parcel's appraised value.

Carter County's website carries a notice titled 2026 Carter County Property Reappraisal Notice: What Homeowners Need to Know. A reappraisal can move values for many parcels at once and can lead the county commission to reset its tax rate. If your value changed, call the assessor and ask what the new appraisal is based on, and ask the Trustee what rate applies to your 2026 bill.

Tennessee applies the same assessment ratios in every county: 25 percent of appraised value for residential and farm property and 40 percent for commercial and industrial. Multiply the assessed value by the rate per $100 to get the tax. The county commission sets the rate each year, usually with the budget adopted around July.

How much is Carter County property tax on a typical home?

Elizabethton's rates page lists a county rate of $2.03 and a city rate of $1.57 per $100 of assessed value. Confirm the current figures with the Trustee, because the rate can change in a reappraisal year.

When are Carter County and Elizabethton taxes due?

County taxes become payable on the first Monday in October, and the last day to pay the preceding year's taxes without interest is the last day of February, with delinquency starting March 1, according to the Tennessee Comptroller's schedule. Elizabethton runs a later calendar for city taxes.

  • Card payments to the city carry a 1.89 percent fee plus a 50 cent transaction fee.
  • The city clerk cannot waive interest, penalty or court costs under state law.

If you do not receive a notice for each parcel you own in the city, call the property tax clerk at 423-547-6205. The city says notices are a courtesy, since state law does not require them, so a missing bill does not excuse a missed deadline.

How do you appeal a Carter County property assessment?

Start with the county board of equalization. Tennessee's Comptroller says the board generally convenes June 1 and hears appeals of the assessor's current-year values. Contact the Assessor of Property at 423-542-1801 for the meeting place, an appointment and the current-year filing deadline.

An assessment generally must be appealed to the county board to keep the right to appeal further. After that, a taxpayer can go to the State Board of Equalization. The state's deadline is August 1 of the tax year or 45 days from the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. The state schedule also shows that the assessor can correct clear clerical errors in coding, ownership, location or physical description before March 1, up to the second year after the tax year in question.

Keep any written value evidence, such as a recent appraisal or a sale of a comparable house nearby, and bring it to the assessor's office when you ask for an appointment.

Two other state dates matter for owners with land or rentals. The deadline to apply for greenbelt classification is March 15, and the deadline to apply for exemptions is May 20. Owners of business property, including equipment in a rental business, receive personal property schedules by February 1 and should return them by March 1.

What relief, delinquent tax and closing rules apply in Carter County?

Tennessee's tax relief program reimburses low-income elderly and disabled homeowners and disabled veteran homeowners or their surviving spouses for part or all of the local taxes paid. It is not an exemption, you still get a bill, and only the primary residence qualifies. Applications are available at the county Trustee's office and the city collecting official's office. Elizabethton adds that prior-year city taxes must be paid or eligibility is lost.

The county Trustee's page says taxes over 13 months past due must be settled through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, and tax sales are run by the Carter County Clerk and Master. For a payoff on a delinquent parcel, call the Trustee at 423-542-1811.

On a sale, the city's guidance is direct. A buyer or seller who closes after January 1 still sees the bill go to the owner of record as of that date, and the closing statement should deduct the former owner's pro-rata share. Taxes are a lien on the real property, and the purchaser is responsible for checking that earlier years were paid.

Carter County sits in the Blue Ridge Mountains, with Roan Mountain, at 6,285 feet, on the border with North Carolina. The Census Bureau counts about 57,361 residents, 28,715 housing units, a 75.2 percent owner-occupancy rate and a median household income of $50,135, so tax relief matters in a county where 24.1 percent of residents are 65 or older.

Call the Assessor of Property at 423-542-1801 or use the real estate assessment data link on the county's assessor page. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

Who handles delinquent Carter County taxes?

The Trustee handles delinquent questions at 423-542-1811. Taxes more than 13 months past due go through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, which also runs tax sales.

Do I still owe tax if I get state tax relief?

Yes. The Tennessee Comptroller says relief is a state reimbursement, not an exemption. You receive the bill, pay it, and the state reimburses you for all or part of the taxes paid.

Madison County by the numbers

Which Madison County offices handle property tax?

Three offices share the job, and none of them does all of it. The Assessor of Property values the land and buildings, the County Commission and the Jackson City Council set rates, and the Trustee collects the county's bill. The assessor's own page says the office neither sets the rate nor collects tax.

  • Trustee: Billy Burkhead, 100 E. Main St., Suite 107, Jackson, TN 38301, phone (731) 423-6027, open weekdays, 9:00 to 5:00, on the courthouse's first floor.
  • Assessor of Property: Frances Hunley, Suite 304 on the courthouse's third floor, phone (731) 423-6063, open weekdays, 8:30 to 5:00.
  • City of Jackson Revenue Office: bills tax for houses inside the city. A city address owes both the county and the city.

The county's Payment of Taxes page says the Assessor's office neither accepts payments nor mails bills. It supplies owner names and mailing addresses to the offices that do, so a moved owner should update the address with the Assessor.

What does the Madison County landscape look like to a seller?

Madison County lies in West Tennessee, and Jackson is its seat and its biggest city. It was founded in 1821 and named for James Madison. It covers 559 square miles, nearly all land, and borders Gibson, Carroll, Henderson, Chester, Hardeman, Haywood and Crockett counties. Interstate 40 crosses it along with US 45, US 70 and US 412.

Several landmarks shape how people describe the area. Pinson Mounds, one of the largest Woodland period mound complexes in the country, lies in the county, and Lake Graham, a 500-acre reservoir, sits five miles east of Jackson. Beyond Jackson, the county includes Medon, Three Way, Beech Bluff, Pinson and parts of Humboldt and Mercer. The Jackson-Madison County School System serves public school families, Lane College and Union University are in the county, and West Tennessee Healthcare runs the public hospital system. Jackson Regional Airport took that name in 2025.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Madison County:

  • Population on July 1, 2025: 100,790, versus 98,823 at the 2020 census
  • Housing units: 44,744, with 62.0% owner-occupied from 2020 to 2024
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $211,800

When does the next Madison County reappraisal happen?

The next reappraisal is set for 2027, and the last one was in 2022. The Assessor's page cites Tennessee Code 67-5-1601 as the reason the county has to reappraise on a schedule. Madison County works on a five-year cycle, and between cycles the office inspects about one-third of the parcels each year for changes to land or buildings.

The office posts a market indicator on that page. It reports a median residential sale price of $251,450 as of January 2026, against $212,500 at the 2022 reappraisal, which it describes as roughly an 18.33% rise. That gap is the main reason an owner should expect a higher appraised value in 2027. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value and commercial property at 40 percent, per the county's FAQ.

Assessment Change Notices go out by law, usually in May, and only to owners whose value moved up or down from the prior year. Notices that come back undeliverable are common, so owners who moved in the last two or three years should call the office to fix the address.

When are Madison County tax notices sent, and how do I pay?

Notices should reach owners in the first week of October, and the Assessor says taxes cannot be paid early. Search and pay online at paymadisontaxes.com, call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 or stop by the courthouse. The Trustee's site notes that the office collects only county property tax, and the County Commission sets the rate.

Tennessee taxes follow the owner of record on January 1 for the whole year. That means the county's public records will not show a mid-year purchase on the new owner's tax bill. The Assessor's FAQ also warns that tax figures on a closing statement are typically estimates, especially for a closing before October 1, and tells buyers and sellers to ask the closing attorney who pays what. For the delinquency date and interest schedule, ask the Trustee directly, since both are set by the county's collection office.
