How do I appeal a Madison County assessment?

First call the Assessor at (731) 423-6063 and ask to verify the property record. The office reviews the property card, takes down your reasons, and has a field appraiser recheck it. If that does not settle it, the next step is the Madison County Board of Equalization.

The board is five property owners from the county and the City of Jackson. By law it hears appeals on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, and the county begins scheduling appointments in the last two weeks of May. One FAQ elsewhere on the county site says the board sits for the first week to ten days of June, so confirm the dates with the Assessor. The board can only hear the current tax year: the county's example is that 2025 taxes cannot be appealed in 2026.

The county asks residential owners to bring comparable sales from the year or two before the tax year, a recent paid appraisal and photos of the exterior and interior. Owners of income property are asked for three years of leases, rent rolls, income and expenses, appraisals, sales contracts, closing statements and construction costs. Refusing to supply those documents can cost the right to introduce them before the State Board. The appeal page adds that the State Board filing carries a fee, with $10 to $17 of it nonrefundable, and that you must pay at least the undisputed part of the tax before it turns delinquent. The State Board's number is 615-401-7883.

What tax relief does the Madison County Trustee offer?

The Trustee takes applications for the state's relief program for elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans. Call the Trustee's office at (731) 423-6027 for the current requirements.

Applicants should bring a driver's license, a Medicare card, a Social Security card and proof of income for the applicant, spouse and every owner of the property. A mobile home owner also needs a copy of the title or bill of sale. Because the dollar limits change from year to year, ask the Trustee for the current income cap and filing deadline before assuming you qualify.

What should a Madison County seller do about tax before closing?

Ask the Trustee, and the Jackson Revenue Office if the house is in the city, for a written balance before you list. The January 1 rule means the owner of record on that date is the name on the bill even after a fall closing. Whether the buyer reimburses the seller for the unexpired months is something the closing attorney settles on the statement.

Sellers with older balances, an estate to settle or a pending appeal can raise those items with the closing attorney before the contract date. Paying an old balance first keeps the file simple and prevents a delay at the table.

Yes. A house inside Jackson owes Madison County tax through the Trustee and City of Jackson tax through the city's Revenue Office. A house outside the city limits owes the county tax only.

The January 1 owner stays on the county's records for the entire year, so the bill may carry the seller's name after closing. The closing attorney divides the cost between buyer and seller, and the Assessor suggests asking that attorney how.

About two weeks in June. The county page says hearings run on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, with appointments taken in the last two weeks of May. Call (731) 423-6063 for this year's schedule.

Where do McMinn County owners go with property tax questions?

Tax bills come from the Trustee, and value questions go to the Assessor of Property. The Trustee works from the courthouse in Athens, and the County Commission sets the rate.

The Trustee's page lists the three jobs of the office: collecting county property tax, keeping the county's accounts, and investing idle funds. Tax notices are mailed in October to whoever owned the property on January 1, and the owner is responsible for keeping the mailing address current with the Assessor.

What is McMinn County like for a homeowner or seller?

McMinn County sits in East Tennessee, and Athens is both its seat and its biggest city. It was created in 1819 and named for Governor Joseph McMinn. It covers 432 square miles of Ridge and Valley country, where long parallel ridges run northeast to southwest. The Hiwassee River marks the line with Bradley County, and Starr Mountain rises in the southeast along the edge of the Cherokee National Forest.

Besides Athens, the county holds the cities of Etowah, Niota and Sweetwater, the towns of Calhoun and Englewood, and Riceville. Railroads shaped the early map: the East Tennessee and Georgia line ran through in the 1850s, Etowah grew around an L&N depot, and Englewood became a textile town. In 1946, returning World War II veterans confronted county officials over a disputed election in the Battle of Athens.

School lines matter here. McMinn County Schools runs most of the public schools, including McMinn County High and McMinn Central High. Athens City Schools and the Etowah School District cover grades K to 8 in their own areas, with the county's high schools taking those students after eighth grade. Tennessee Wesleyan University is in Athens.

When are McMinn County property taxes due?

Payment opens October 1 and stays open through the last day of February without penalty. Today is November 15, 2026, so the current year's tax is already payable. On March 1 the Trustee adds 1.5 percent per month in penalty and interest to unpaid tax.

Mail is accepted, and the postmark sets the payment date, with a receipt returned by mail. Delinquent tax is a lien that follows the parcel to any owner, so buyers are urged to run a title check for liens. The county also requires delinquent taxes to be paid before current ones, which means a prior-year balance absorbs a payment aimed at this year's bill.

The office also opens on Saturday mornings in February. For payment methods beyond mail and in-person, call (423) 745-1291.

How can a McMinn County owner dispute a value?

Start with the Assessor of Property, then file with McMinn County's local equalization board. State law sends a disputed value to the county board before anything else, and a case that skips it generally becomes final. The Comptroller's appeals guide explains that the county board is a panel of five or more people who hear complaints and can change disputed assessments.

  • County board: file by the date the Assessor gives you for this year's session.
  • State Board of Equalization: on August 1, or on the 45th day after the county board mailed its notice if that is later.
  • Hearing: before an administrative judge, with a written decision within 90 days after the hearing.
  • Chancery court: a petition within 60 days after the state board's order is final.

McMinn County's FAQ adds one point for business owners. A forced assessment, which happens when a business fails to file a personal property schedule, can be set aside only by an appeal to the local board before that year's deadline. The county's FAQ says the schedule is due before March 1.

What property tax relief exists for McMinn County owners?

The Trustee administers a state-funded program for elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans. When an applicant qualifies, the State of Tennessee pays a portion of the tax on the home. The Trustee's page says an application must be filed no later than 35 days after the February 28 payment deadline, which lands in early April. The FAQ also mentions programs for veterans with a 100 percent rating.

Because income limits and credit amounts are set by the state each year, call (423) 745-1291 for this year's figures before you apply.

What should a McMinn County seller know about tax at closing?

Old tax stays with the house, so a buyer's title search will find any unpaid year. The county says delinquent tax binds the property whoever owns it, and a seller with a late balance should expect the title company to require payoff at closing.

Ask the Trustee for the amount for each tax year, including interest, before you accept an offer. If the house is inherited, behind on payments or in need of repairs, the tax balance is one more number the title company will collect from the proceeds, and knowing it early keeps the closing date from slipping.
